interest: This file offers historians an exceptional insider perspective on Axis diplomatic and intelligence relations during World War II, revealing the deep strategic divergences and mutual distrust that undermined German-Japanese collaboration. Rather than demonstrating a monolithic alliance, Classen's interrogation illustrates how Japanese Embassy officials in Berlin were split between Ambassador Oshima's dogmatic pro-Nazi stance and pragmatic factions led by Naval Attaché Admiral Kojima and Counselor Kawahara, who recognized Germany's impending collapse and urgently sought German-Soviet rapprochement or an 'Asia-pact' to protect Japan's rear against the United States. Additionally, the documents provide valuable organizational insight into the German Intelligence Service's Far Eastern networks, detailing the SD's covert exploitation of academic bodies like Berlin University's East Asian Institute, cryptanalytic intercepts of Swiss and Turkish diplomatic cables from Chungking, and the operational use of commercial intermediaries, double agents, and Vlasov army officers.
overview: This file (decimal 894.20262/4-1046) consists of an April 10, 1946 transmittal letter from FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover to Frederick B. Lyon of the Department of State, forwarding records derived from the November 2, 1945 interrogation of Dr. Wilhelm Classen, a German Far Eastern intelligence expert. The enclosed documents contain a signed statement listing key German Japanologists and two detailed intelligence reports surveying Japanese diplomatic personnel in Berlin and the operations of the German Intelligence Service (GIS) regarding East Asia. The reports dissect the internal factions, political maneuvers, and pro-Soviet inclinations of Japanese diplomats and military attachés—contrasting Ambassador Hiroshi Oshima's rigid pro-German orientation with Naval Attaché Admiral Kojima's advocacy for Japanese-Soviet cooperation—while detailing German espionage sources, cryptanalytic intercepts of foreign diplomatic traffic in Chungking, academic research covers, and intelligence liaisons across Berlin, Hamburg, Shanghai, and Lisbon.

subfiles.about: Transmittal letter from FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover forwarding copies of an interrogation report and statement of Dr. Wilhelm Classen concerning the Japanese Embassy in Berlin and German intelligence collaboration.
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover - Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.summary: FBI Director John Edgar Hoover transmits a personal and confidential letter by special messenger to Frederick B. Lyon, Chief of the Division of Foreign Activity Correlation at the Department of State. The letter encloses copies of a statement and report derived from the November 2, 1945 interrogation of Dr. Wilhelm Classen. Hoover highlights that the documents provide details on the Far Eastern Department of the German Intelligence Service (GIS) and its collaboration with the Japanese Embassy in Berlin and Japanese intelligence networks.
subfiles.title: Letter from J. Edgar Hoover to Frederick B. Lyon Transmitting Interrogation Report on Japanese Embassy in Berlin
subfiles.to: Mr. Frederick B. Lyon, Chief, Division of Foreign Activity Correlation, Department of State

subfiles.about: Signed statement by Dr. Wilhelm Classen identifying key German Far Eastern and Japanese experts, their professional backgrounds, and potential contact locations.
subfiles.summary: In this signed statement, Dr. Wilhelm Classen provides information on four German specialists on Japan who could be useful contacts for Allied authorities. He profiles Legationsrat Dr. K. O. Braun of the Foreign Office's Far Eastern Department, Karl Zahl, former General Secretary of the German-Japanese Society, and RSHA Japanese expert Joern Leo, detailing their language abilities, political outlooks, and likely post-war whereabouts in Berlin, Bad Gastein, and Schiltach. Classen also lists himself as a professor at Heidelberg University and offers to assist in contacting them.
subfiles.title: Statement of Dr. Wilhelm Classen on German Far Eastern Experts

subfiles.about: Interrogation report of Dr. Wilhelm Classen evaluating the personnel, internal factions, and political attitudes of the Japanese Embassy in Berlin toward Germany and the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: Dr. Wilhelm Classen provides a comprehensive evaluation of Ambassador Hiroshi Oshima and key staff members of the Japanese Embassy in Berlin. He describes Oshima as an uncritical adherent of National Socialism whose optimistic reporting was discounted by the Tokyo Foreign Office, which relied instead on reports from Ambassador Suma in Madrid and Ambassador Sato in Moscow. Classen analyzes the opposing viewpoints of embassy counselors Kawahara and Uchida, both of whom favored rapprochement with the Soviet Union and China, and highlights Naval Attaché Admiral Kojima's strategic view that Japan needed peace with Russia to confront the United States, alongside sketches of press attaché Dr. Oga and commercial liaison Sakai.
subfiles.title: Interrogation Report on the Personnel and Factions of the Japanese Embassy in Berlin

subfiles.about: Interrogation report of Dr. Wilhelm Classen outlining the structure, informants, cryptanalytic services, and operations of the German Intelligence Service concerning East Asia.
subfiles.summary: Dr. Wilhelm Classen details the sources and methodology of the German Intelligence Service (GIS) regarding the Far East, including the Japan-Gruppe within RSHA Amt Mil and Abwehr branches in Shanghai and Hamburg. He assesses the reliability of various domestic informants, such as Admiral Richard Foerster of the German-Japanese Society, Dr. Donat's covert East Asian Institute at Berlin University, antique merchant Nakanishi, and Dr. Otto Richter of the Ostasiatischer Verein. Furthermore, Classen reviews high-grade intelligence derived from OKW cryptanalytic deciphering of Swiss and Turkish diplomatic traffic from Chungking, Foreign Office reports leaked by Dr. Braun, Portuguese police liaison in Lisbon, and Russian officers of the Vlasov army.
subfiles.title: Interrogation Report on the Far Eastern Department and Sources of the German Intelligence Service
